title: Light
standard_text: Identify natural and artificial sources of light; describe how light travels in straight lines and is reflected, absorbed or transmitted by materials; describe uses and effects of light technologies. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand C: Matter and Energy – Light and Sound)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 science worksheets on light sources, transparent, translucent and opaque materials, shadows, reflection and refraction. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Materials let light through, let some through or block it; shiny surfaces reflect it.
body_html:
How to think about it

Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines.

  • Natural light sources: the Sun, stars, lightning, fireflies. Artificial sources: bulbs, flashlights, candles.
  • Transparent materials let light through; translucent let some through; opaque block it and make shadows.
  • Light reflects (bounces) off shiny surfaces and refracts (bends) when it moves into water or glass.
  • The Moon is not a light source: it reflects sunlight.
Example

Is wax paper transparent, translucent or opaque?

some light passes through

you cannot see clearly through it

Answer: translucent

Example

Why does a shadow form?

light travels in straight lines

an opaque object blocks it

Answer: the object blocks the light

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the Moon makes its own light.
  • Thinking shiny objects like mirrors are light sources.
  • Mixing up translucent and transparent.

faq.q: What is the difference between reflection and refraction?
faq.a: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Refraction is light bending as it passes into a different material.
Light from a source reflects off the object and travels in a straight line into our eyes.
Looking at the Sun can damage eyes, and too much artificial light at night can confuse birds and insects.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a candle flame, a glowing computer screen, a shiny spoon or a star?
items.e: A shiny spoon does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a candle flame, a cat's eye reflector on a road, a lit bulb or a star?
c: a cat's eye reflector on a road
items.e: A cat's eye reflector on a road does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which material is transparent?
items.e: Transparent materials let almost all light through.

items.q: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. Why?
c: Light bends (refracts) as it passes from water to air.
items.e: This is refraction.

items.q: Which material is translucent?
items.e: Translucent materials let some light through.

items.q: Why are some lights near lakes turned down or shielded at night?
c: Bright lights can confuse birds and insects.
items.e: Light pollution affects animals.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a flash of lightning, a glowing computer screen, the Sun or the planet Venus?
items.e: The planet Venus does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Is a glowing computer screen a light source?
c: a light source only at night
not a light source: it reflects light
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these is a light source: a bicycle reflector, a cat's eye reflector on a road, a glowing computer screen or a mirror?
c: a cat's eye reflector on a road
items.e: A light source gives out its own light. The others only reflect light.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a campfire, a flashlight that is switched on, the Sun or the planet Venus?
c: a flashlight that is switched on
items.e: The planet Venus does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which is an artificial source of light?
items.e: People make artificial sources.

items.q: Which is a natural source of light?
items.e: Natural sources are not made by people.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a bicycle reflector, a campfire, a flash of lightning or a flashlight that is switched on?

items.e: A bicycle reflector does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these is a light source: a bicycle reflector, a mirror, a sheet of white paper or a flashlight that is switched on?
c: a flashlight that is switched on
items.e: A light source gives out its own light. The others only reflect light.

items.q: Is a sheet of white paper a light source?
c: a light source only at night
not a light source: it reflects light
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

items.q: In a room with no light at all, could you see a red ball?
c: Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, a little, because objects glow.
Yes, if it is shiny or white.
items.e: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Dark is the absence of light.

items.q: Is a flashlight that is switched on a light source?
c: a light source only at night
not a light source: it reflects light
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

c: No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
Yes, if it is shiny or white.
Yes, a little, because objects glow.
items.e: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Dark is the absence of light.

items.q: Is the Moon a light source?
c: a light source only at night
not a light source: it reflects light

items.q: In a room with no light at all, could you see a bright yellow raincoat?
c: Yes, a little, because objects glow.
No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
Yes, if it is shiny or white.

items.q: Leah shines a flashlight at a clear jar. What happens to the light?
c: It lets all the light through.
items.e: A clear jar lets all the light through.

items.q: Sofia wants to make curtains to make a bedroom dark. Which material is best?
items.e: It needs a material that blocks the light.

items.q: Sofia holds a clear jar in a beam of light. What will the wall behind it look like?
items.e: A clear jar lets all the light through.

items.q: Is a brick transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: A brick lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Priya holds clear plastic wrap in a beam of light. What will the wall behind it look like?
items.e: Clear plastic wrap lets all the light through.

items.q: Why does a cyclist wear a reflective vest at night?
c: It reflects car headlights so drivers can see the cyclist.
items.e: Reflectors bounce light back.

items.q: Is a thin cotton sheet transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: A thin cotton sheet lets some light through, but you cannot see clearly through it.

items.q: Aiden shines a flashlight at clear plastic wrap. What happens to the light?
c: It lets all the light through.
items.e: Clear plastic wrap lets all the light through.

items.q: Is the Moon a source of light?
c: Yes, it makes its own light.
No, it reflects light from the Sun.
items.e: We see the Moon because it reflects sunlight.

items.q: Light hits a mirror and bounces off. What is this called?
items.e: Smooth shiny surfaces reflect light well.

items.q: Chloe holds a hand in a beam of light. What will the wall behind it look like?
items.e: A hand blocks the light.

items.q: Noah shines a flashlight at frosted glass. What happens to the light?

items.e: Frosted glass lets some light through.

items.q: Is a metal tray transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: A metal tray lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Nathan shines a flashlight at a mirror. What happens to the light?
c: It lets all the light through.
items.e: A mirror bounces the light back.

items.q: Is a plastic milk bottle transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: A plastic milk bottle lets some light through, but you cannot see clearly through it.

items.q: Is aluminum foil transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: Aluminum foil lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Zoe wants to make a box to keep film in the dark. Which material is best?
items.e: It needs a material that blocks the light.

items.q: Ethan holds a thin paper plate in a beam of light. What will the wall behind it look like?
items.e: A thin paper plate lets some light through.

items.q: Benjamin wants to make a fish tank so you can see the fish. Which material is best?
items.e: It needs a material that lets all the light through.

items.q: A student drew this model to show how a person sees an apple (the red circle) next to a lamp. Is the model correct?
c: No. The light should start at the lamp, not at the object.
No. There should be no lamp.
Yes. It shows the light correctly.
No. Light only travels in curves.
items.e: Light comes from the lamp, not from the object to the lamp.

items.q: The red circle is a teddy bear in a room lit by a lamp. Which diagram shows how a person sees the teddy bear?
items.e: Light goes from the lamp to the object, bounces off (reflects) and enters the eye. Diagram C shows light coming out of the eye, which is wrong.

items.e: Light goes from the lamp to the object, bounces off (reflects) and enters the eye. Diagram A shows light coming out of the eye, which is wrong.

c: a hand shape with spread fingers
items.e: Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the same outline as the object.

items.e: Transparent, translucent, opaque.

items.q: Which material would make the darkest shadow?

items.q: A material lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it. Which word describes it?
items.e: Transparent, translucent, opaque.

items.q: A material lets no light through and makes a dark shadow. Which word describes it?
items.e: Transparent, translucent, opaque.

items.q: A flashlight shines on a tin can standing upright, seen from the side. What shape is its shadow?
c: a hand shape with spread fingers
items.e: Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the same outline as the object.

items.q: A flashlight shines on a cube facing the flashlight. What shape is its shadow?
c: a hand shape with spread fingers
items.e: Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the same outline as the object.

items.q: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
items.e: Opaque materials block all the light.

items.q: A flashlight shines on a coin facing the flashlight. What shape is its shadow?
items.e: Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the same outline as the object.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 55° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a black sock, a polished silver tray, a sheet of aluminum foil or a still pond?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 60° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a mirror, a piece of black paper, a sheet of aluminum foil or a still pond?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: A ray of light goes from air into a glass block at an angle. What happens or why?
c: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water.
Different colours refract by different amounts.
It bends away from the normal.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 65° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is. What happens or why?
c: It bends away from the normal.
Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water.
Light refracts as it leaves the water.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: What is one danger of light?
c: Looking at the Sun can damage your eyes.
items.e: Never look straight at the Sun.

items.q: A shadow forms when …
items.e: Shadows are areas with no light.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a black woolly sweater, a glossy white tile, a mirror or a shiny metal spoon?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: A ray of light comes out of a glass block into air at an angle. What happens or why?
c: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water.
It goes straight on without bending.
It bends away from the normal.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: A ray of light enters a glass block along the normal (at 90° to the surface). What happens or why?
c: Light refracts as it leaves the water.
It goes straight on without bending.
Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a bicycle reflector, a lump of black coal, a new coin or a shiny metal spoon?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 30° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: Which of these reflects the most light: a dark carpet, a muddy soccer, a piece of dark brown cardboard or a still pond?
c: a piece of dark brown cardboard
items.e: Smooth, shiny and light-coloured surfaces reflect the most light.

items.q: How does light travel?
items.e: That is why shadows form.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 50° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 70° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: Which of these reflects the most light: a lump of black coal, a muddy soccer, a navy blue towel or a shiny metal spoon?
items.e: Smooth, shiny and light-coloured surfaces reflect the most light.

items.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 25° to the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror). At what angle does it reflect?
items.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

items.q: Why do eye doctors say children should play outside but wear a hat in strong sun?
c: Daylight is good for eyes, but strong sun can harm them.
items.e: Balance.

items.q: Why is it easier to find a white sock than a black sock in a dim room?
c: White reflects more light into our eyes.
items.e: Light colours reflect more.

items.q: Noah uses two mirrors to make a periscope. What does it let him do?
c: see over a wall by reflecting light twice
items.e: Each mirror reflects light toward the next, and then into his eye.

items.q: Lucas says the moon makes its own light because it glows at night. Which fact shows he is wrong?
c: The moon's lit side always faces the sun.
items.e: The bright part is the part that sunlight is hitting.

items.q: Which pair of objects are both sources of light?
c: the sun and a lit candle
a mirror and a lamp that is off
items.e: Sources make their own light.

items.q: A pupil says a cat can see in complete darkness. Is that right?
c: No, cats cannot see at all.
No. Cats need a little light, though they see well in dim light.
items.e: All eyes need light.

items.q: A window is made of frosted glass. Why?
c: It lets light in but people outside cannot see clearly in.
items.e: Translucent.

items.q: Ava puts a toy in a shoebox with the lid closed and looks through a small hole. She cannot see the toy. Then she opens a second hole to let light in. What happens?
items.e: Light enters through the second hole, reflects off the toy and comes out to her eye.

items.q: How could you show that light travels in straight lines using a hose pipe and a flashlight?
c: Use a pipe in the dark only.
Shine the flashlight through a straight pipe and then a bent pipe and compare.
items.e: Straight pipe: light gets through.

items.q: Hana and a teddy bear are in a room with no windows and the lights off. There is no light at all. Can she see the teddy bear?
c: Yes, if she looks very hard.
Yes, because her eyes send out light.
Yes, after her eyes adjust for a long time.
No. No light can reflect off the teddy bear into her eyes.
items.e: We need light to reflect off an object and enter our eyes. In total darkness, there is nothing to see.
